title: The #1 Deal-Killing Mistake Buyers & Sellers Keep Making
content: Hi, I'm Sarah Sharp. I'm a deal attorney who helps people buy and sell businesses every day, and I would like for you all to stop killing all the deals by having this one type of meeting. So it is negotiation season over deal academy. A lot of our deals are currently in the process negotiation, and I, as you guys know, like to track the data as much as possible. There are a ton of deals that have died this year, and there's a correlation or a causation between the deal death and the type of meeting that happened that killed it. So I'm hypothesizing that this one deal mistake, as one meeting mistake will kill your deal. Either correlative or causative, it remains to be seen. So there are some good meetings. When we're doing some different negotiation, I see all kinds of meetings that help move things along. Typically the process of negotiation is it relates to the transaction documents, which are where all of the deal points should live. Those start out like this. The buyer initiates a draft, so the buyer hires a lawyer to pit together a purchase agreement. They go over it with their lawyer in a lot of detail. The primary objective is to make sure that it matches the letter of intent, and also the parties' subsequent communications, if anything, in the deal terms have changed. Then we go over to the seller with the, we're on the buy side, we send those transaction documents to the seller, and it solicits their feedback. So, seller, what do you think about this? The seller usually will review it themselves before they even send it to their council and point out anything that's kind of the business terms, like the dollars are wrong, or this is not the interest rate we talked about that kind of thing. And once they've ironed out any deal term considerations, then they send it to their attorney. In their attorney, hopefully, hopefully, please guys, just makes Microsoft redline changes to the word document and sends it back, but often they do some other way of telling you their changes, whether it's an email bullet point list, whether it's a printout, jpeg of their scrolled suggested questions and handwriting that you can't read, whether it's this very annoying lawyer software called litra, no representation connotation here, because I don't like it. And it's this very old school, in my view, software that takes your changes and makes a PDF summary of them that then you have to use to compare against your word document and decide what changes you want to accept or reject. You need 6,000 monitors to effectively take in all of the information of that type of comparison document, but whatever way they want to carry your pigeon back, the seller's changes and proposed changes to the buyer they do. And then you're in a situation where you have the buyer's proposal and the seller's essentially rejection. And you've got to figure out with council as the buyer, what do I accept and what can I not live with? And I always tell my clients at the beginning of a call, if I'm the buy side, this is where we want to accept 75% or more of the changes if we want the deal to go through, because I do accounting practice buyouts and I have really smart clients. And they're not asking for things that are crazy. So we want to keep it moving. Also, because I do usually deals under $10 million, most of my clients are also running a business at the same time that they're selling. So you do not have time or bandwidth or interest in infinite rounds of negotiation between lawyers and the legal fees will start to eclipse what's reasonable for a deal of that size if you let it go on too long. So once you've got those red lines in the initial draft, let's try to accept 70% or more. And if there's something that we can't accept at that point, it fits in two buckets. It's either a deal point where the business parties need to get on a call and iron it up because there's maybe not a meeting of the minds. They just hadn't thought about it. They hadn't talked about it yet or they've changed their mind for something like maybe they realize they really need the seller to stick around and help them for the first tax season after closing. The number one mistake that people make that kills deals at this stage is suggesting an all-hands meeting. Do not suggest an all-hands meeting. It's so often the death knell of a of a transaction and of the negotiation. And it comes from such a very understanding place, right? We think, well, I have some things I need to talk about with the business parties. You have some things you need to talk about, well, we all hop on a call, but lawyers suck. We are the worst. And the dynamic is not a good one. And in all hands meeting for it to actually lead to any kind of conclusion that people feel good about because you have two different lawyers on the same side. They work well because they've got a professional deal team leading them. They've got business people who are, you know, pretty much as competent as any lawyer in the legal documents and also have been really trained in negotiation and rapport building. So they are navigating the heck out of it. No lawyer is performing, hopefully, and the sell side is just there to learn. Sometimes those can be a good way, especially to cut through where you maybe need to gently as the buyer educate the seller in the seller's attorney that it's a take-it-or-leave-it proposition. And that can be hard to do in writing and sometimes sellers wind up with an attorney who doesn't do a lot of this and doesn't kind of advise them of the respective negotiating power of the parties in the way that they should and so to level set that type of all-hands call can be an effective way to say, listen, you're not going to build a make-any progress on any term changes to any of this agreement. description:
If you're in the middle of buying or selling a business, especially an accounting firm, this is the video you cannot afford to skip.

In this video, I’m pulling back the curtain on the one meeting format that consistently blows up deals mid-negotiation.

In this video, you'll:

✅ Learn how negotiation should go
✅ Know what your lawyer should be doing (and what they shouldn’t)
✅ Understand why “all hands” meetings are the kiss of death in small business M&A
✅ See how to save time, legal fees, and your sanity

Whether you're a buyer, seller, or just fascinated by what actually kills deals in the real world, this one's for you.

For more information on Deal Academy, a program that teaches you how to buy and sell accounting practices, click the link here:
https://www.dealacademy.org

To connect with Sara Sharp on LinkedIn:
https://www.linkedin.com/in/sara-sharp-9a2a98b/

For more information on our Mergers and Acquisitions law practice click here:
https://www.skandslegal.com
